In a used copy of *Middlemarch*, I once found a grocery list pressed between pages 312 and 313: eggs, thread, batteries, aspirin. Someone had needed those things badly enough to write them down, then lost the list to George Eliot, and eventually lost the whole book—or chose to let it go.

This is the quiet afterlife of secondhand books. They carry cargo we never intend. Dried flowers flattened into paper memories. Phone numbers without names, digits that now dial nothing. A teenager's furious underline through a sentence about death, made by someone who is perhaps no longer furious, or alive. Margin notes arguing with authors who cannot answer: "No—" and "Yes!!" and, once, memorably, beside a passage on grief, simply "me too."

Reading their traces, I become an eavesdropper across decades. This stranger underlined the lines I would have chosen. They paused where I pause, stumbled at the same stubborn paragraph, quit dog-earing page two hundred and abandoned the journey—as I nearly did, until their ghost made me curious enough to go on.

And here is the stranger truth beneath it: all reading works this way. Every book reaches you down a tunnel of prior eyes; even the first reader after the author hunches over the author's shoulder. Used books merely make visible what reading usually hides—that nobody ever reads alone. We are constantly finishing one another's sentences, borrowing one another's lamps.

Someone once needed aspirin. Now I think of her whenever Eliot writes about pain.
